blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we meet two amazing movers.
Our first hero has four legs, but it is not a dog.
It climbs mountains, wades through icy rivers, and never gets tired.
Our second hero is smaller than your thumb, yet it can do something no other bird on Earth can do.
Let's go!
High on the stone steps of Mount Tai in China, a line of pedestrians stops and stares.
Coming up the steps is a robot dog with a heavy bag on its back.
These robot dogs work as mountain porters, carrying heavy loads so human porters can rest.
One robot dog, called B2-W, can carry forty kilograms and walk fifty kilometres on one charge.
Cheers erupt as it arrives at the top.
Another robot dog, called Lynx, works high on a cold mountain, where the air is thin and it is thirty degrees below zero.
It climbs slopes as steep as forty-five degrees, splashes through icy rivers eighty centimetres deep, cold spray flying around its legs, and keeps its balance.
Its cameras have sharp discrimination: they can tell a safe rock from a loose one.
The robot's patience never runs out: it can try the same steep path again until it finds a safe way up.
They are quick, too.
One of them, called HOUND, holds a world record: it ran one hundred metres in less than twenty seconds.
They are ambassadors for a new kind of helper.
On a mountain, it is a champion.
Now meet a bird with a great trick.
The hummingbird is no bigger than your thumb, and it drinks sweet nectar from flowers.
Most birds must turn around to leave a flower.
Not the hummingbird.
It simply flies backwards, straight out of the flower.
It is the only bird on Earth that can do this.
The secret is in its wings.
Most birds flap up and down, and only push air on the way down.
A hummingbird's wings move in a figure eight — they push air on the way up and on the way down, too.
Its wings can beat fifty to eighty times every second.
Its shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, like yours, so its wings can turn in every direction.
A hummingbird's flight muscles make up nearly one third of its body.
It must eat all day, and males even fight over the best flowers.
Its throat shines like a diamond in the sun, vivid green and red.
When it flies away, its soft hum fades into the garden.
Evolution gave this tiny bird a wonderful gift: wings that can carry it forwards, backwards, and even upside down.
Here's today's idiom: "keep an eye on." It means to watch something or someone carefully.
The engineers keep an eye on the robot dog as it climbs the mountain.

Here's an example: "Please keep an eye on my little brother while I buy the tickets." So, keep an eye on things you care about — and keep an eye on the hummingbird, too, or it will zoom away before you blink!
Let's think about our stories.
We met robot dogs that climb mountains in freezing cold, and a tiny bird that flies backwards.
First: if you had a robot dog, what job would you give it?
Second: if you could fly like a hummingbird, where would you fly first — forwards or backwards?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Keep an eye on the little wonders around you — and keep exploring.
See you tomorrow morning!
